clue.text: Sly boasts must supply evidence of wealth

definitions.note: singular phrase for a plural answer: the things that show off wealth

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple, the preceding words bend flexibly into a new order

parts.note: letters taken as written for the mix
also part of the mix, despite looking like a link

explanation.surface: Crafty bragging is required to prove someone is rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like a verb but is the adverb from supple, pronounced SUP-lee; 'must' pulls double duty as surface verb and fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Status symbols are possessions such as flashy cars or watches that display a person's riches and social standing.

clue.text: Halfwit gets in early to see poet

indicators.note: something that gets in goes inside, so the halfwit sits within the other word

parts.note: early in the sense of before long
a fool, a silly person

explanation.surface: A dim-witted person arrives in good time to visit a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Siegfried Sassoon was a First World War poet; S(ASS)OON.
explanation.definitionFit: Siegfried Sassoon is a famous English war poet, so the surname is an example of a poet.

clue.text: This actor wants to get away

definitions.note: a phrase read as what an actor desires, not a synonym
definitions.meaning: first meaning: an actor wants a role in a play, said as two words
second meaning: separated, at a distance

explanation.surface: A performer is desperate to escape.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as A PART, it is what any actor craves; run together it means separated, as in 'set apart'.
explanation.definitionFit: Apart describes being at a distance from others, just as away does, e.g. living apart.

clue.text: Enthusiastic usurer initially obtaining obscene profit

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of usurer

indicators.note: something obscene is indecent and twisted, so the next word's letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written for the mix

explanation.surface: A greedy moneylender is keen to make an indecent return.
explanation.definitionFit: Being up for it is an informal idiom for being keen and willing to take part.

clue.text: Here you might rest with 'Paddington Enters Armed Forces'?

definitions.note: a description of a place, standing for a plural noun

indicators.note: what enters goes inside, so the London terminus is placed within the military word

parts.note: the army, navy and air force are collectively the services
Paddington is a London railway terminus

explanation.surface: A newspaper headline about the famous bear joining the military.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddington is a bear but here a London station; SERVICE(STATION)S. Service stations are roadside stops on motorways.
explanation.definitionFit: Service stations are motorway stops where drivers pause for fuel, food and a break from driving.

clue.text: Financier Bernie did this with the loot, we're told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it, so the spoken form is what counts

parts.note: a thief made off with the loot, meaning ran away with it

explanation.surface: A jibe that a notorious fraudster absconded with stolen money.
explanation.walkthrough: Bernie Madoff ran a huge Ponzi scheme, so the surface joke is close to the truth.
explanation.definitionFit: Bernard Madoff was an American financier jailed for running a vast investment fraud.

clue.text: A heap, old boy? Not a sausage

parts.note: surface reading: a chummy greeting, then the idiom for nothing at all
setter's reading: a heap is a decrepit car, and the phrase for one sounds like an aged sausage, which it is not

explanation.walkthrough: A banger is a sausage in Britain, and 'not a sausage' is slang for nothing; a heap is a rundown old car.
explanation.definitionFit: A heap is slang for a battered, worn-out car, which is exactly what the British call a clapped-out motor.

clue.text: Unseemly exchange by railway is quite a sight

parts.note: making a scene is a public row
RY is the abbreviation for railway
placement word: the next piece goes beside

explanation.surface: A row on the platform is quite a spectacle.
explanation.definitionFit: Scenery is a view of landscape that one admires, often a striking view worth looking at.

clue.text: Section of atlas, I assume!

indicators.note: a section is a slice, so the letters lie within the following words

parts.note: runs across the end of atlas, the I and the start of assume

explanation.surface: Someone guessing which page of a map book they are looking at.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the continent is indeed a section of any atlas.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia is a continent, and every world atlas devotes a chapter of maps to it.

clue.text: Degrader of transportation?

indicators.note: transportation moves things from place to place, so the letters are carried into new positions

parts.note: every letter used in the mix

explanation.surface: A question about who damages public transport.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: someone dodging the ticket price lowers the railway's takings.
explanation.definitionFit: A fare dodger travels without paying, cheating and undermining the bus or rail network.

clue.text: Health expert let fish go bad after flipping

indicators.note: flipping turns things over, so both words are read back to front

parts.note: a common sea fish
to decay

explanation.surface: A dietitian allowed some fish to spoil.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor is a medical practitioner, a professional whose expertise is keeping people well.

clue.text: Find out about unusual radiation

definitions.note: the answer is usually an adjective, used here as the noun for the radiation itself

indicators.note: about means around, so the shuffled word goes round the next part
out as in out of order, so the word before it is scrambled

parts.note: taken as written for the mix
uncommon

explanation.surface: An instruction to investigate some odd emission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Find out' looks like a phrase meaning discover, but out is the mixing signal; INF(RARE)D.
explanation.definitionFit: Infrared is electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible light, felt as heat.

clue.text: Actor — Alec Guinness, say — given line

parts.note: Sir Alec Guinness was knighted, so he is an example of one
a ley line is a supposed alignment of ancient sites

explanation.surface: A famous actor is handed a line of script.
explanation.walkthrough: Alec Guinness is the obvious actor to define, but he is only an example of a titled man; the definition is the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Keira Knightley is an English film actress, so her surname serves as an example of a performer.

clue.text: Ultimately, visiting Arizona, Illinois, Long Island and Ontario is big deal

definitions.note: a huge number, loosely a great deal

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the next word

parts.note: the closing letter of visiting
US state postal code
US state postal code
the usual abbreviation for the New York island
Canadian province postal abbreviation

explanation.surface: A grand North American road trip described as a major undertaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Gazillion is an informal word for an enormous, uncountable amount, a great deal of something.

clue.text: Unappealing, lousy (on the outside)?

indicators.note: the outside of a word is its first and last letters, applied to both preceding words

parts.note: the first and last letters
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A judgement that something looks bad on the surface.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: something unattractive looks lousy from outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Ugly means unpleasant to look at, so outwardly poor and unattractive in appearance.

clue.text: Head of Blackpool Zoo, bumbling buffoon

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of Blackpool

indicators.note: bumbling means clumsy and muddled, so the next word's letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written for the mix

explanation.surface: A seaside zoo director is an incompetent fool; Blackpool is a resort town in northwest England.
explanation.definitionFit: A bozo is American slang for a stupid or clownish person, much like a buffoon.

clue.text: Campaigns against 'having area for old wine collection'

indicators.note: having one thing for another means a swap, putting the first in the second's place

parts.note: standard abbreviation for area
standard abbreviation for old
a stock of wine is kept in bottles

explanation.surface: Someone lobbying to stop a wine cellar being given extra space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'area for old' is an instruction: put A where O was in the wine word.
explanation.definitionFit: To battle against something is to fight or struggle to oppose it, like campaigning against it.

clue.text: You've let me down, putting rotten butter on butties regularly

indicators.note: rotten food has gone off and broken down, so the next word's letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written for the mix

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters; butties are British slang for sandwiches
placement word: the next piece follows

explanation.surface: A sandwich-maker reproached for spreading stale butter.
explanation.walkthrough: Caesar's dying words to his friend Brutus in Shakespeare, quoted to anyone who betrays you.
explanation.definitionFit: Et tu, Brute? is the reproach to a trusted friend's betrayal, the classic cry of being let down.

clue.text: Hunt: pro renewal of Humberside etc

indicators.note: a renewal remakes something, so the words before are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: every letter used in the mix

explanation.surface: A politician named Hunt backs regeneration of a northern English region.
explanation.walkthrough: Humberside is a former county on England's northeast coast, around Hull.
explanation.definitionFit: Up north is the British idiom for the northern regions of England, which include Humberside and its neighbours.

clue.text: Vacant twit in tutu's dancing, getting sounds of disapproval

indicators.note: dancing moves things about, so the combined letters swap places
vacant means emptied, so the inside of the next word is removed leaving its outer letters

parts.note: the word with its middle cleared out
taken as written, the apostrophe ignored
joining word: the two lots of letters combine

explanation.surface: An airhead pirouetting in a ballet skirt draws clucks of disapproval.
explanation.definitionFit: Tut-tuts are clicks of the tongue made to express mild disapproval or annoyance.

clue.text: Sordid affair that's seen at evening classes

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun

indicators.note: sordid suggests something dirty and messed up, so the next word's letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written for the mix

explanation.surface: A seedy romance between people who met on an adult education course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sordid affair' reads as one idea, but sordid is only the mixing signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffia is palm fibre used for weaving baskets and hats, a staple material of adult craft classes.

clue.text: Committed saint with extremely abnormal verruca

parts.note: standard abbreviation for saint

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the next word, its first and last letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of abnormal
a verruca is a wart on the foot

explanation.surface: A devout holy man afflicted with a strange foot growth.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalwart is loyal and dependable, someone committed to a cause or team.

clue.text: Dishevelled, untidy, in state of undress

indicators.note: dishevelled means messy and disordered, so the next word's letters are tangled

parts.note: taken as written for the mix

explanation.surface: Someone scruffy and messy, caught half-dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Nudity is the condition of wearing no clothes, being naked.

clue.text: Every so often, DJ is sick of dance music

indicators.note: every so often means at intervals, so alternate letters are kept

parts.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: A record spinner occasionally gets fed up with club tracks.
explanation.definitionFit: Disco is a style of upbeat 1970s pop made for dancing in clubs.

clue.text: Part of Yorkshire fighter rose for the audience?

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the words are taken by their sound

parts.note: a fighter is a military aircraft
a rose is a flower

explanation.surface: A Lancaster-versus-York tale: a fighter and the white rose of Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of Yorkshire' suggests a district, but it is an ingredient of Yorkshire pudding, a baked batter side dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain flour is the basic ingredient of the batter for Yorkshire pudding, so it is one of its components.

clue.text: Compact weapons withdrawn

indicators.note: withdrawn means pulled back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: firearms

explanation.surface: A treaty in which arms are pulled back.
explanation.definitionFit: Snug means cosily small and tight-fitting, a close sense of compact.

clue.text: Religious instruction fervently shuns cold soya

definitions.note: singular phrase for a plural answer

indicators.note: fervently suggests passionate agitation, so the following words are stirred up

parts.note: every letter used in the mix

explanation.surface: A churchy food lesson where someone firmly refuses chilled soy.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunday schools are church classes teaching children the Bible and faith, a form of religious teaching.
